lessons.title: Greetings & Introductions
lessons.blurb: Say hello, introduce yourself, ask how someone is.

grammarNote.title: Formal (vy) vs. informal (ty)
grammarNote.text: Czech has two ways to say "you": ty (informal — friends, family, children, peers your age) and vy (formal — strangers, officials, anyone older or in a professional context). This isn't optional politeness, it changes the verb ending too: jak se máš? (informal) vs. jak se máte? (formal). When in doubt, default to vy — Czechs will tell you if they'd rather switch to ty.

check.prompt: You're meeting your new landlord for the first time. Which greeting fits?
check.explanation: „Dobrý den“ is the formal, safe greeting for anyone you don't know well — landlords, officials, shopkeepers.
check.note: „Ahoj“, „čau“, and „nazdar“ are all informal — fine for friends, wrong for a first meeting with someone you should address formally.

check.explanation: „Jmenuji se“ actually means "My name is" — it's how you introduce yourself, not how you ask someone else's name (that's „Jak se jmenujete?“).
check.note: „Jmenuji se“ and „Jak se jmenujete?“ share the verb jmenovat se ("to be named") but one is a statement about yourself, the other a question.

check.prompt: How do you say "thank you" in Czech?
check.explanation: „Děkuji“ (or informally „díky“) means "thank you". „Prosím“ means "please" or "you're welcome".
check.note: „Prosím“ and „Děkuji“ are a natural pair — you'll use them together constantly, so it's worth memorizing both from lesson one.

lessons.title: Numbers 0–100
lessons.blurb: Count, tell time, and understand prices.

grammarNote.title: Numbers 21–99 are built like German
grammarNote.text: Czech builds compound numbers "ones-and-tens", the reverse of English: 21 is dvacet jedna (twenty-one, said as two words) but many learners find it easier to think of it the way German speakers build numbers — the unit often gets glued to the ten with no "and": jedenadvacet (one-and-twenty) is an older but still-used alternative form. For everyday use, the simple dvacet jedna, dvacet dva… pattern (ten-word then unit-word) is what you'll hear most and is safest to use yourself.

check.explanation: „Padesát“ means fifty. „Patnáct“ (not padesát) means fifteen — a very common mix-up for beginners.
check.note: „Patnáct“ (15) and „padesát“ (50) look and sound similar to new learners — say them out loud a few times to build the distinction.

check.prompt: Type the Czech word for the number 10.
check.note: Numbers 1–10 are the foundation for everything else (prices, time, dates, ages) — worth over-learning before moving on.
